cues.text: Section five: the service lifecycle.
Let us now turn to the traditional ITIL version 3 lifecycle.
This is also taught in this session, and it consists of five stages.
It is important that you do not confuse it with the service value system found in ITIL 4.
They are two different ways of organizing service management, so keep them separate in your mind.
Here are the five stages, in order.
The first stage is service strategy.
Here the organization identifies its customers, the business outcomes they need, the demand for services, and its investment priorities.
The second stage is service design.
In this stage, the organization defines the functionality of the service, along with its availability, security, capacity, continuity and support requirements.
The third stage is service transition.
Here the organization tests, releases and deploys changes, and it does so with the support of configuration management and knowledge management.
The fourth stage is service operation.
This is where services are actually delivered.
The organization monitors performance and resolves incidents and service requests.
The fifth stage is continual service improvement.
Here the organization measures results, identifies gaps, and implements improvements.
To see how these stages fit together, consider a university launching an online examination portal.
In service strategy, the university identifies reliable remote assessment as the desired outcome.
In service design, it specifies authentication, capacity and accessibility requirements.
In service transition, it tests the portal under peak load and trains the support staff.
In service operation, it monitors examinations while they are running and resolves any failures that occur.
Finally, in continual service improvement, it uses incident reports and student feedback to improve future examination sittings.
Notice how each stage builds on the one before it, and how the last stage feeds back into improving what comes next.
